title: Hardy Opens a Letter From Madras
text:
In January 1913 G. H. Hardy, one of the leading mathematicians in England, received a letter at Trinity College, Cambridge, from a clerk in the Madras Port Trust in India. The writer, Srinivasa Ramanujan, explained that he had no university degree but had been working on mathematics on his own. Enclosed were pages of formulas and theorems, many stated without proof. Ramanujan had already written to other Cambridge mathematicians, who had not taken him seriously.

Hardy nearly put the letter aside as the work of a crank. That evening he went over it with his colleague J. E. Littlewood. Some of the results were known; some were wrong; but others were unlike anything they had ever seen. Hardy later wrote that they must be true, because if they were not, no one would have had the imagination to invent them.

Hardy replied at once and worked to bring Ramanujan to Cambridge, which he did in 1914. For five years the two collaborated on work that changed number theory. Ramanujan was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1918. Ill, he returned to India in 1919 and died the next year at thirty two. Hardy called their collaboration the one romantic incident of his life.
lesson: Take seriously the work of people who lack credentials or connections. Looking twice at something unusual can uncover talent that others dismissed.
people: Srinivasa Ramanujan, G. H. Hardy, J. E. Littlewood
location: Cambridge, England, and Madras (modern Chennai), India
source: G. H. Hardy, Ramanujan: Twelve Lectures on Subjects Suggested by His Life and Work (1940); Robert Kanigel, The Man Who Knew Infinity (1991)
